newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Finnish ERM link heats up Swedish currency debate.
newsitem.headline: Finnish ERM link heats up Swedish currency debate.

text.p: Finland's decision to enter the EU's exchange rate mechanism will intensify the currency policy debate in neighbouring Sweden and may increase pressure on Stockholm to follow the Finnish move, economists said on Sunday.
By joining the ERM, Helsinki showed its determination to be in the first group of countries to join economic and monetary union (EMU) from its planned start in 1999.
If Italy also joins, only the Swedish crown, the British pound and the Greek drachma would remain outside the grid, which now groups 11 of the European Union's 15 currencies.
"Finland has now become a precedent and this will put pressure on Sweden," said Carlo Erakallio, chief economist at Handelsbanken Markets Finland.
A Stockholm-based economist took a similar view.
"This increases pressure on Sweden to link the crown to the ERM," he said. He saw it has a 50/50 chance that it would happen already this year.
However, others disagreed, saying a Swedish currency link would not take place soon.
"I think it is very, very unlikely that we do see a Swedish krona link, at least for the time being," said James McKay, international economist at Paine Webber in London.

Senior economist Knut Hallberg at Swedbank said Sweden would probably wait until parliament decided in late 1997 about joining monetary union. But he said there was also a possibility that a link could happen early next year.

Widespread public opposition to the single currency in Sweden may make it politically difficult for the Social Democratic government to link the crown to the currency mechanism as it could be seen as a step towards EMU membership.
Because of this, some believe the country may also decide to bide its time on EMU membership even if it were to qualify by meeting tough economic conditions on government debt and borrowing.
"The Swedish position is governed almost totally by domestic politics," said McKay at Paine Webber.

Currency stability is also a criterion for EMU and several countries, including EU heavyweights France and Germany, argue that the EU's Maastricht treaty requires ERM membership in order to qualify for the single currency.
By joining ERM, "Finland is going to have greater chances of being sure to fulfil all of the criteria," said Johnny Akerholm, under-secretary of state at the Finnish finance ministry.
However, Sweden and Britain say it is currency stability, not ERM membership in itself, which should be the key for being able to take part in monetary union.
On Saturday, Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink insisted the Finnish ERM-link did not affect Sweden and there was no reason to change its monetary and currency policies.
"It is the government's view that it is not on the agenda for Sweden to link the crown to the ERM," Asbrink said.
However, Central Bank governor Urban Backstrom last month indicated he believed it would be desirable to join the ERM, saying it could underscore increased economic stability.
But he stressed it was important to have public support in Sweden for any decision to join the currency grid.

The two Nordic nations, which both joined the EU in January last year, are major trading partners as well as fierce competitors on world markets in pulp and paper. Their currencies have been floating since Europe's currency turmoil in late 1992.
